title: Jungian Psychology and Buddhism
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The main teaching of the Soto Zen dharma talk is that true understanding and freedom from suffering are not easily attainable, but by embracing the present moment and letting go of our conditioned minds, we can cultivate a deeper awareness of ourselves and the world around us. This involves recognizing the impermanence and interconnectedness of all things, including our own thoughts and emotions, and finding ways to balance our desire for safety with our need for growth and change. By doing so, we can begin to transcend our limitations and find a more authentic and fulfilling way of living.

sentences.text: *An unsurpassed, penetrating, and perfect dharma is rarely met with even a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having yet to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagatas.*
Good evening, everybody.
I miss getting to hear everybody say good evening back on these little things we don't have on Zoom.
Yeah, that's it.
We have a lot, don't we?
The mind so easily drawn to what we lack.
Okay, I'll speak a little louder.
Thank you for the request, Nusama.
How's this?
Can you hear me okay?
Okay, cool.
All right.
Well, good evening again.
Here we are back to our non-practice period mode on Wednesday evening: zazen, kinhin, service, a talk with some discussion, a lot like Sunday at 10.
One difference is that on Sunday we're alternating teachers, and Chris is doing such a great job inviting folks inside and outside the sangha who can give dharma talks to share with us on Sundays.
Wednesday will be mostly me doing some series of talks for the most part.
And then also the first Wednesday of the month, practicing the precept ceremony.
Where I go on a few sangha housekeeping items.
One is a big thank you to everyone who spent some time with the visioning survey, the online survey, with reflections and visions about the future of Red Cedar.

If you haven't done that yet, it'd be great if you could do that soon.
You probably want to set aside a half an hour or so.
I realize the best might be to open it up, and there's a link in your email or there's a special web page I'll mention in a minute where you can get all the details.
But anyway, what you might do if you haven't done it yet is open it up and read over the questions, and then shut it again and muse and sleep on it and think about it on a walk or something.
That might be nicer than just sitting at the computer trying to visionify on demand.
Anyway, the overall project is called a campaign, campaign onward go to Zen soldiers, I guess.
And so we made a special page, Red Cedar Zen dot org slash campaign.
That's where the repository of all the stuff is.
It's like a private web page.
It's not linked in anywhere.
You just have to be in the know in the sangha, and the emails mentioned that.
And further, just a reminder that we'll spend the morning together, hopefully as many of us as we can, on Saturday, the 27th, nine to noon.
It's both our usual annual meeting, hosted by the board of directors to update us on how things are going at an organizational level.
But in this case that part will be brief, and it will mostly be discussion of this vision, facilitated by Thomas Bruner.
He's a charming fundraising consultant and facilitator who works with Buddhist groups to do this kind of stuff.
So anyway, that's the two things that are going on.
And maybe we'll hear at the end about other things going on, and start having announcements again at the end for sure.

I'm looking forward to spending several weeks in a row exploring something about the neuroscience perspective on how the mind creates our experience, or responds to our experience, or responds and creates our experience.
But I scheduled that to start next week for some reason, which I can't remember.
But I had another topic I want to explore.
So we'll do that tonight.
Just have a single talk for now on the topic of Jungian psychology.
I don't claim to be any kind of expert on Jungian psychology, but a friend of mine put me onto a book, which I'm finding super fascinating.
The way the Jungians, at least as exemplified by this particular author, talk about the mind and about our conditioning just feels very supportive and similar to the Dharma.
At least to one major aspect of the Dharma, of our Buddhist training, Buddhist practice.

One aspect of that is to really explore and understand and clarify our craziness, our conditioned aspects, the way who and what and how we are has been created and generated partly by cause and effect, through society, family of origin, environment, everything.
And we've got that to practice with.
But that all by itself is kind of crazy-making, right?
Because it's sort of like our conditioned mind trying to figure out our conditioned mind, which is a fabulous hamster wheel.
So luckily we have a second aspect of Dharma practice, Dharma understanding, which is the layer of emptiness, or the unconditioned, or boundlessness, or freedom, nirvana, space, spaciousness.
We reference that constantly when we chant the Heart Sutra, which is so shorthand it's hard to make any sense of it.
But in the Heart Sutra, you know how they use negation: no eyes, no ears, no nose, no thoughts, no this, no that.
All the standard Buddhist terms are buried in there, and they're all negated.
Negation not meaning negation, but meaning not what you think it is, meaning bigger than that, meaning empty: empty of any fixed solid anything.
It reminds us that not just the senses and Buddhist concepts are fluid and not bounded, so boundless, empty of inherent existence.
Not just those things, but everything is that way.
Everything is empty, which means everything is free.
So it's strange language for a really beautiful, stunningly beautiful sensibility or idea.
And we only have language to talk about all that, to talk about this empty, unconditioned, non-dual side of things.
And language is kind of inherently dualistic, right?
Language is inherently this or that, and this is pointing to something bigger than this or that.
So in Zen we go on about that a lot.
We study it a lot in various ways.

I thought we'd just spend a minute on that to remember that when we get into the nitty-gritty of different models of our conditioning, which is what this Jungian stuff is, a very interesting model of our conditioning, there's more than that.
That's just one half of a coin.

And since we just did the Heart Sutra, I thought we could also dip our toes into the Diamond Sutra, which takes the super abbreviated cryptic language of the Heart Sutra and expands it out a little bit.
So here is the pith exchange in the Diamond Sutra.
This is a monk named Subhuti talking to the Buddha.
And this is condensed too.
In the Diamond Sutra, this famous text on emptiness, Subhuti asked the Buddha, if a noble son or daughter sets forth on the Bodhisattva path, how should they behave?
How should they practice?
How should they think?
And the Buddha says, they should think this thought, Subhuti.
They should think this way.
*However many beings there are in every realm, I shall liberate them all.
And though I thus liberate countless beings, not a single being is liberated.*
And why not?
He goes on, anticipating that we're all scratching our heads: why is it that although I liberate countless beings, not a single being is liberated?
*Well, Subhuti, a Bodhisattva to whom the concept of a being occurs cannot be called a Bodhisattva.
Why?
Because no one called a Bodhisattva would conceive of a being or a life or a soul.*
Of course, it goes on with many variations of that for many pages.
What great quirky stuff, this tradition we've received.
It takes a little getting used to, but we've all been working on getting used to this kind of language.
Not just getting used to it, but feeling the depth and beauty of it too.

This way of talking is a way of reminding us that on this empty, unconditioned, open side of our lives, or this penetration through our lives of all that, things are so vast, so wide open, that they could never be limited by concepts or words, or calling this of this and that of that, this of being and that of Bodhisattva.
That would just be way too limiting and too diminishing for the beautiful reality that we live in.
You could also call this the absolute layer of our practice.
Things are absolutely beyond concepts.
So the thing about that is there's not much to hang your head on, you know what I mean?
Everything's beyond concepts.
What do we do?
How do we practice?
Well, we sit zazen, which is a non-conceptual practice.
We're not told, sit zazen and figure out your problems.
Sit zazen and review the day and see what you did wrong and think about what you're going to do tomorrow.
We sit just to sit.
So that's a very direct way we actually practice this non-conceptual, non-conditioned, boundless, absolute, whatever you want to call it, realm.
But the idea is that the best for us is to operate in both of these realms together, in harmony with each other.
To feel in our hearts, little by little, let it seep in.
It takes decades apparently, many more probably than any of us have practiced, to really let this seep in, to really be able to trust fully the unconditioned nature of our living.
But within that feeling, to get busy and to be smart, to get curious, to understand our conditioning as best we can.
To understand that against this vast, peaceful, free background of the unconditioned means that we don't have to get upset about it so much.
It can be interesting.
And even when we get a little tripped up by it, when we come out of it at least, we can say, oh, geez, and have a little humor about it.
We can have a little peace about it and take it seriously.
Like this is also, the conditioned is the source of all suffering too, untold suffering through the generations and the millennia.
And the unconditioned is also a place of great joy and delight and creation and newness, right?
So anyway, here's a model that might be helpful.
I'm finding this really interesting and I hope you find it helpful too.
And ironically, as you'll soon see, I'm feeling anxious about bringing it up because, yeah, what am I?
I'm not a trained Jungian analyst.
I just read this book, but I did read it a couple of times and thought about it.
So I'm just going to go for it because I think it's helpful.
But the reason why it's ironic that I feel anxious will be clear in a minute, and I'll talk more about that then.
So I'm going to be unpacking some stuff from a book by a Jungian analyst named James Hollis.
Here's the book.
The title of the book is Finding Meaning in the Second Half of Life: How to Finally Really Grow Up.
We're at various ages.
Many of us might consider ourselves either before or after half of life.
Maybe I'm somewhere, I don't know how you say what half is.
But I think it's actually all pretty universal.
That's just his main audience for the book.
And the other thing is that after some decades of life and going through some stuff, maybe we're ready.
Maybe we're ready to take a fresh look at the way we are and grow up.
And maybe we have to go through stuff.
We have to survive our lives in various ways and work hard and get bound up about this, that or the other and get through things.
And somewhere in midlife we have some resources and some possibilities to learn more about who and what we are.
Here's how he says that.
It's nice.
So I hope regardless of your age you can appreciate this sentiment.
I'm going to quote him a bunch, so I'll just do a sort of quotation-y voice.
He writes a lot differently than I do, so hopefully you'll be able to tell when it's James Hollis and when it's me.
He writes,

*The second half of life presents a rich possibility for spiritual enlargement, for we are never going to have greater powers of choice, never have more lessons from history from which to learn, will never possess more emotional resilience or more insight into what works for us and what does not, or a deeper and sometimes more desperate conviction of the importance of really living our lives, being alive.*
A couple of terms are helpful.
Self in Jungian land is kind of like Suzuki Roshi's big self.
So when they say self, it's Jung's metaphor for the inherent, unique, knowing, directive intelligence that lies beyond our ordinary ego consciousness.
So self is an expansive self.
And ego in this is ordinary self-awareness, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah.
Kind of a little smaller: Suzuki Roshi's small self.
He also talks about the soul.
And we just heard the Diamond Sutra try to negate the existence of a soul.
But he says, and I assume this is Jungian orthodoxy, that actually the word psyche is Greek for soul.
So what's wrong with the word soul?
Psyche being the root, right, of psychology and all the different related disciplines that are the study of the self.
So the soul is kind of the bigger context.
That which the self is seeking is the soul or the psyche: deeper meaning, purpose, greater-than-self understanding.
So maybe for soul or psyche we might say Buddha nature or maybe Bodhicitta.
And here's an example sentence about the soul.
He says,
*A life that constricts meaning wounds the soul.*
So the soul is sort of organic.
Souls are a sense of our great possibility.
A soul is a sense of our awakening.
He gives a little background before he gets into this model, and I think it's pretty interesting.
He says it's really worth not losing track of where we came from, which is a womb, right?
We should never underestimate the powerful moment of birth.
So we study birth and death, and that's big here too.
At birth we're plunged out of comfort and safety into a very uncertain world, and our ego is born from this sense of separation.
He says that our lives always hang by a slender thread.
Before consciousness, that thread was the umbilical cord to our mother, our source.
And then that gets cut, right?
That gets separated.
We're all coping fine.
We're all doing all right.
But in this system, they really encourage us to look into that, feel into that, feel into the sort of primordial depth of separation.
And look at all the mythology and all the stories and all the religions, and of course, especially obvious in Christianity, about this: the sense of fall, the sense of separation.
The Adam and Eve story is that they were all blissed out in the garden, right?
Until partaking of the tree of knowledge brings the mixed blessing of consciousness, of self-awareness, traumatic and a great gift.
From that moment, we're driven to try to figure this out.
How can I survive?
How can I thrive?
On the one hand, there's this deep urge to move forward and to learn and to grow and to be self-sufficient.
And there's this contrasting drive to get back somewhere safe.
To get back to the garden, get back into the womb.
There is a tension there, and that tension in Jung land is a neurosis.
Neurosis is not all bad, because it's information.
It's something for us to study and look at.

And all development involves some kind of separating, some kind of differentiation, some sort of individuation, some sort of moving out of our previous comfort, our previous, whatever safety we've managed to find or was provided to us.
We also vary a lot, of course, and they allow for this, in how much support we had, whether we had a safe, high attachment childhood or more traumatic childhood.
But he points out, yes, that's true for sure.
Some of us are less challenged by this separation and the challenge of growing up into the world.
But all of us, no trauma, just inherent, it's just baked into our human development.
What that ends up setting us up with for the rest of our lives is a dynamic, a little challenge or a big challenge, between safety and growth.
A few quotes from James Hollis about this.

*Fear of further departure, fear of the unknown, fear of the challenge of largeness, intimidates us and can scare us back into our convenient rituals, our convenient thinking and our familiar surroundings.*
Another place he writes, this is great:
*Each morning, the twin gremlins of fear and lethargy sit at the foot of your bed and smirk.
Are you going to be able to get up today?*
I don't mean to make light of this.
I know some of us have friends and relatives where those gremlins are really powerful.
It's really hard to get out of bed, for sure.
But all of us are working with this dynamic.
The point he makes over and over and over again is that that's true whether we know it or not, whether we know it or not, that's happening.

And so this [unclear: "whole brain"], studying this, and if you were really into this, going into Jung, working with the Jungian therapist to explore all this, or just studying the models we're trying to do tonight, is to daylight these processes.
So they happen more within our awareness, so we have more choice, we have more choice.
And I think we do, through Zazen and through our practice, create a life and a situation where that increased awareness and that daylighting of unconscious process does become a lot more possible.
Sometimes it's a joyful thing that we have realizations, and things are clear to us that were not clear to us before, through our practice.
Other times I think that process operates in a way that's pretty challenging, maybe disturbing.
During this last sesshin I spent a morning or so just dipping into this kind of deep heaviness and hardness and fear.
I feel like there's a certain kind of that that I only ever noticed during sesshin, and it must be there all the time, that deep kind of unhealed, whatever it is, at the bottom.
So this stuff feels to me very simpatico with Zen training, for sure.
But here's the thing.
Every one of these choice points, he says, and I think this is worth exploring, choice points in life involve a choice between anxiety and depression.
Isn't this cheerful?
Anxiety is the choice of growth.
Of course we're going to feel anxious, so this is like good anxiety, the anxiety of challenge, the anxiety of choice.
And depression is in this system associated with falling back, kind of regression, falling back into safety.
Might be that something around sort of self care and rest and self compassion, somewhere in the middle there, is a little bit missing, at least the way I read him.
But that's okay, no model needs to be complete, because no model can be complete, right?
Because these are just models.
But this is a good challenging model, I think, for us to practice with: to wonder, whenever we're a little anxious about a choice, whether we can look at it from these lenses.
Is there a path here that's a path of growth and change and healing, and entering into a bigger possibility in my life?
So this big self, is there a big self choice here?
And if there is, it would not be surprising if I'm feeling anxious about it and I don't want to do it.
Versus, is there a choice here that's shutting down, that's falling back, that's not living my life to my potential?
And [unclear: "he says he's having all the time"].
He writes:
*This archetypal drama between anxiety and depression, growth and retreat, is renewed every day, in every generation, in every institution, and in every decisive moment of personal life.*
Big statement, it's everywhere, he says.
And it plays out in every moment of our lives, whether we recognize it or not.
And these choices create our patterns, the values of our daily lives, and our variegated futures.
And the good choice in this model is going for it.
It's choosing anxiety and ambiguity, for these are the developmental choices.
And so that lands with Buddhism, that lands with not knowing, that lands with what a mystery this life is, right?
We can never know.
So to move towards the unknown, move towards the ambiguous, move towards this growth choice that has a quality of anxiety to it, and that we can choose that as service, he writes.
So here's the Bodhisattva path. [unclear: "Alice writes"]:
*The struggle for growth is not for us alone.
It is not self-indulgent.
It is our duty and service to those around us as well.
For through such departures from the comfortable, we bring a larger gift to others and to ourselves.*

The thing I think is really interesting about this kind of stuff is how easy it is to just read this stuff and think about this stuff or hear this stuff, in your case right now, and just take it in intellectually and say, yeah, it makes sense, or I'm not so sure about that, but to hold it as a conceptual thing out here.
And maybe what's dynamic for us between the conceptual and non-conceptual is when we actually land it, when we actually notice that, oh, here it is actually happening in me.
I just got a little baby taste of that this afternoon and evening preparing this talk.
I noticed this anxious voice in me saying, you don't know what you're doing.
Why don't you do a [unclear: "call on talk"] or something?
What is this about this stuff?
You setting yourself up or something?
Maybe I should just scrap this whole thing.
I almost scrapped the whole talk a couple of times.
And then it was only later, actually, as I was putting on my robe, as Kate was doing the [unclear: "haunt"], so maybe [unclear: "our forums help us"],
I thought to myself, oh, my gosh, of course, that's the anxiety he's talking about.
I guess I better give this talk.
Yeah.
So it's interesting how hard it is.
And this is true with our practice for sure, too, right?
We hear these teachings and we can write them down and agree with them and like them or not like them or read more books about them and so on and so forth.
But it takes quite a bit of time and the right conditions and a little luck maybe to get to where they actually enter your heart, where you actually practice them and inhabit them.
Because nobody wants to be anxious, right?
Nobody wants to be challenged, really prefer to be comfortable.
And yet to be comfortable all the time, it's kind of a dead sort of life.
We don't want that either.
And he says we have to really watch out for hubris.
They like Greek mythology and Greek terminology in this Jung land.
So hubris is not pride, though.
He says hubris really means our temptation to believe, that we wish to believe, the assumption that we know all we need to know about ourselves and the situation to make wise choices.
So hubris is a kind of blind spot, thinking we know who we are, thinking we know what's happening.
We know for sure practice has helped all of us soften from that viewpoint, because also we notice that we suffer more when we're super sure of ourselves.
So that's hubris.
That's a factor we hold in mind with this model, and that our view is conditioned.
They say, in a very similar way to Buddhism, that the way we view things is like a lens we look through. [unclear: "I live uses my metaphor to"], he writes:
*At birth, each of us is handed a lens by our family of origin, our culture, our zeitgeist, through which to see the world as it is, the only lens we have ever known.*
So we presume that we see reality directly, even as we are seeing reality colored and distorted.
So I've always loved practice for this, too.
The teachings can give us another lens.
I think the precepts are particularly powerful that way.
If you haven't done our precept study group, we have one starting at the end of the month, actually.
With the precepts, we take up different lenses to look at our lives through, and we see different things.
It's really quite remarkable.
And of course, sitting Zazen, we see the results of our lenses generating all those thoughts and stuff in our heads all the time.
So anyway, how do we work with all this?
Well, we practice, and we practice with others.
The [unclear: "communion"] quotation here is:
*Only the corrections of others or the corrections of our violated psyche may oblige us to consider that our fundamental way of seeing and understanding is suspect.*
So we would say, study your suffering.
That's the violated psyche.
And study with a teacher and study with sangha.
So we have this opportunity to receive corrections from others.
And of course, Shantideva is very big on this.
So that's another thing that we're going to start studying again.
Chris has offered us a little bit of practice.
So that was mostly background.
Now I want to share with you a list of six responses to this sort of tug of war within us, this being born into an uncertain world, the sort of fundamental way of seeing and understanding.
So that's the last thing we're going to start studying.
We've all, like I say, we've all adapted reasonably well and we're all functioning and so on.

Here, as the Jungians believe, and he has all these interesting case studies in the book too, like I really believe it, and it fits with our, it fits with, especially with the kind of Yogachara philosophy about, remember, the storehouse with all the seeds that come up, that a lot of what's moving us around is not, we're not aware of, it's not conscious.
So this list of six responses, divided into two groups, is stuff that mostly happens unconsciously, but can severely affect our lives and limit our lives.

What he's saying in the book is we're more likely to be able to work with this and figure it out and actually sort of approach it in mid-life more than we could have when we were younger, but I wouldn't mind knowing about the stuff when I was a little younger.
It might have helped.
But it's a process of making the unconscious more conscious.
Okay, so here's the list of six things that I want to invite us to look at together.
I'm going to put it in the chat too, so it'll be up as a list as well.
There are two groups because he feels, or the Jungians feel, there's sort of two major ways that we feel the trauma of existence, existential trauma.
The two big ways are we feel overwhelmed, which he cutely calls overwhelming, and we feel insufficient.
So this makes perfect sense, right?
The world is an overwhelming place, and maybe we forgot, maybe we don't always notice that anymore, but the world is absolutely an overwhelming place, no question about it.
It's totally logical to feel insufficient.
Am I good enough or smart enough or well-resourced enough to navigate this overwhelming world?
I tell myself I am some days, but do I really feel that way?
Is there some deep, unconscious stuff around all this?
OK, so the first three of the six responses are more related to feeling overwhelmed.
The first response to feeling overwhelmed is to retreat: to hide, to avoid, to procrastinate, to deny, to disassociate.
Quote:
*Who has not forgotten, postponed, disassociated, repressed, or simply fled?
We all have.
And for some, this primitive defense becomes a deeply programmed pattern of aversion to life's large demands.*
As I go through these, let's pause with each one and sit into it for a minute.
We all do all of these, but is one particularly powerful in your life, or has it been?
A response of retreat to the overwhelming nature of reality.
The second one is control, trying to control everything.
It can show up as educational or career choices that are all about finding ways to control what can't be fully controlled.
The control response can be passive-aggressive.
His quote is:
*All of us have endeavored with greater or lesser success to control our environment, less to control us.*
There can be a real urgency when this control response is activated.
Very urgent: I have to get this under control.
I can't tolerate this feeling of loss of control and lack of control.
So let's pause with that for a minute: trying to control things, control yourself, control others, control situations, control systems, control life.
The third of the three responses associated with being overwhelmed is accommodating, which is my personal favorite.
Give them what they want.
He points out how easily this one can be programmed in childhood, that most children learn to get love by providing others with what is demanded or expected or merely implied.

Often people who do a lot of accommodating are perceived as nice and easygoing, likeable, and it's so easy to internalize that in an unhealthy way, so that you spend all your time trying to accommodate everybody else.
He makes the point about the American Psychiatric Association, which writes the DSM, the diagnostic manual, the book on what mental illness is and isn't, with all the categories of mental illness.
He says they actually had a whole conference to consider whether to put this in there under the heading of codependence, which is an accommodating kind of thing.
But according to him, they decided not to because it's way too common.
Making something that normal and common into mental illness would make us all mentally ill, so they couldn't do that.
Plus, what would happen with the insurance companies.
So how can we meet this need, this desire to accommodate, more wisely?
Here's a quote:
*Learning to find one's own truth, hold onto it, and negotiate with others seems easy enough on paper.

In practice, it means catching reflective actions while they occur and suffering the anxiety aroused by acting more consciously in integrity and tolerating the anxiety of [unclear: "assault-driven guilt"] thereafter.*
No guilt from not giving the person what you think they wanted, because in this case it wasn't right and it wasn't true for you.
Maybe we can find ways, he suggests, to make a little more space and consider our responses.
He spent a lot more time on accommodating than the other ones, which was helpful to me since it's my main one.
He dated the book a little bit by giving the example of one of his clients who was really happy when answering machines came out.
Then he realized he didn't have to answer the phone and instantly start accommodating whomever was calling.
He could let the machine take it, think about it, and then call them back the next day in a more thoughtful, measured way.
So maybe we could do the same thing with all of our current communication systems.
He talks about how this pattern, and all the patterns, are so easily reinforced.
You do it once and it helps you feel comfortable or something, so you do it again, and other people reinforce it too.
So that's accommodation.
In response to being overwhelmed, we can retreat, we can try to control the world, we can accommodate.
Three more and then we'll have a conversation.
In response to the wound of insufficiency, feeling ourselves insufficient, he suggests three responses as well.
He talks a bunch about how natural it is.
These are very natural, right?
These aren't stupid.
They're reasonable.
It's just a question of now what do we do about it.
How do we grow up with this reality of it being natural to feel insufficient?
He points out that societal trauma, like poverty, racism, and so on, shows up here in this woundedness.
And this wound of insufficiency tells us that we can't rely upon the world to meet our needs, and that we don't feel like we ourselves are reliable to meet our needs.
So it's really a tough pickle.
The Buddha talks about this too, right?
The deep roots of suffering go so far.
The first response is believing in our undeservingness.
He's kind of going along with the whole thing: because I didn't receive what I needed, that must mean I don't deserve to have my needs met.
He writes:
*Such a person has a tendency to hide out from life, to diminish personal possibilities, to avoid risk, and even make self-sabotaging choices.
One chooses the safe option, be it in work or relationship, rather than the one that challenges and opens new possibilities.*
That's if you feel undeserving.
The unconscious equation here is: I am as I am treated by others.
If I have this belief or this experience that I have been treated as undeserving, then I must be undeserving.
So this is powerful, upsetting stuff for sure.
What he's saying is we all have some of this.
The second response to the wound of insufficiency is overcompensating.
What one lacks internally, one will seek in the outer world.
So this is like going for power.
It's really connected to control.
It's another side of control.
He writes:
*The power complex, the desire for power as a way to overcome the feeling of insufficiency, is found in all of us.
It may propel us to new heights, but it may hurt others along the way.
And it may lead one to reconstruct the very conditions that bring the restoration of the old deficit.*
You end up chasing your tail.
He gives the example of Richard Nixon.
And [unclear: "for not forgotten"] is that Richard Nixon grew up in poverty, that something in his conditioning meant nothing was ever enough.
You all saw that ending.
Narcissism shows up here in overcompensating.
So we have other presidential examples of narcissism.
He has a great little quote from Pearl Bailey.
We had Satchel Paige recently, so now here's Pearl Bailey: "Them's what thinks they is ain't."
That's great, isn't it?
